kurz: How correlation, a number between minus one and plus one, decides whether a mix lowers risk or merely adds costs.

bloecke.md:
The expected return of a portfolio is the weighted average of the individual returns and is obtained by simple addition. This does not apply to risk. Two investments with a volatility of 20% each can, when mixed, produce a portfolio whose volatility lies anywhere between 0 and 20%. Where exactly it lies depends solely on how their deviations from their own means relate to each other. This joint behaviour is measured by the [[Covariance|covariance]].

The covariance is hard to interpret. Its unit is per cent squared, and its magnitude depends on the size of the fluctuations involved. Dividing it by the product of the two standard deviations gives a dimensionless number between −1 and +1. This number is called the [[Correlation coefficient|correlation coefficient]].

bloecke.erklaerung: Correlation is covariance normalised to the interval −1 to +1. The normalisation makes pairs of investments with completely different volatility comparable.
variablen: covariance of the two return series
standard deviations of the two investments

bloecke.md:
At ρ = +1, the two return series lie exactly on a rising straight line; at ρ = 0, there is no *linear* relationship; and at ρ = −1, they move in exactly opposite directions.

There are three things the number says nothing about. First, it says nothing about the slope. An investment that always swings half as much as another still has a correlation of 1 with it. Second, it says nothing about the expected return, because two investments with ρ = −1 can both lose money. Third, it does not capture non-linear dependencies. A position that normally moves independently and only falls along with the rest in a crash shows a correlation close to zero when measured over calm periods.

The variance formula for two investments shows what correlation means for risk.

bloecke.erklaerung: The first two terms are always positive and are fixed as soon as the weights have been chosen. Only the third term, the covariance term, can become negative. The entire mathematical effect of diversification rests on it.
variablen: weights of the two investments, wA + wB = 1
standard deviations of the individual investments
correlation coefficient of the two return series

bloecke.md: Returns are added with their weights; variances are not. The covariance term is the only part of the portfolio variance that you can influence through the combination of investments, and the only one that can become negative. Everything that is called diversification in investment practice aims to reduce this term.

bloecke.titel: Portfolio volatility at 50/50, with 20% individual volatility each
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation in which both investments keep a volatility of 20% and only their correlation changes.

bloecke.md: The smaller part of the effect occurs in the positive range. From ρ = 1 to ρ = 0, risk falls by 29% of the starting value, even though both investments still have a volatility of 20%. Each further reduction in correlation lowers risk all the more, the lower ρ already is. That is why just over 70% of the possible decline falls in the negative range. In real markets, this range is largely theoretical, because investments with a persistently and clearly negative correlation to equities *and* a positive expected return practically do not exist. The second bar shows a case from the other end of the scale. At ρ = 0.87, the measured correlation between US equities and other developed markets, 19.34% of the 20% remains.

The basis is monthly returns from January 2008 to August 2026 in US dollars (Portfolio Visualizer). US large caps had a volatility of 15.67% a year, long-term US government bonds 14.24%. Their correlation was −0.07.

- Contribution of equities: 0.6² × 245.55 = 88.40
- Contribution of bonds: 0.4² × 202.78 = 32.44
- Covariance term: 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 × 15.67 × 14.24 × (−0.07) = −7.50
- Portfolio variance 113.34 → volatility 10.65%

The weighted average of the individual volatilities would have been 15.10%. The mix reduces volatility by 4.45 percentage points without either investment having to give up anything for it. This gap is what is meant by the phrase that diversification is the only free lunch.

bloecke.titel: The same 60/40 portfolio at different correlations

bloecke.md:
The variance contributions of the individual investments stay at 88.40 and 32.44 in every row. Only the covariance term changes. Setting the derivative of the variance with respect to the weight to zero gives the mix with the lowest variance. For these two investments, that is around 46% equities and 54% bonds, with a volatility of 10.16%. This point is the left end point of the efficient frontier. The next lesson covers how a whole curve develops from it.

The last row of the table corrects a common misconception. At ρ = −1, the portfolio does not automatically become risk-free. It becomes risk-free only at exactly one weight, namely wA = σB/(σA+σB), here 47.6% equities. At 60/40, 0.6 × 15.67 − 0.4 × 14.24 = 3.71 percentage points of volatility remain that do not cancel each other out. Perfectly opposite movement alone is therefore not enough; the mix must also be right.

bloecke.titel: Correlation matrix of major asset classes
bloecke.unter: Monthly returns of US ETFs in US dollars, January 2008 to August 2026. For a euro portfolio, the exchange rate shifts these values.

bloecke.md:
## Findings from the correlation matrix

The equity markets of the different regions largely move together. US equities, other developed markets and emerging markets correlate with each other at 0.87, 0.76 and 0.86. Regional diversification therefore barely reduces volatility. It avoids cluster risks in individual countries, currencies and legal systems. That is a different and equally good reason for regional diversification, but not a reduction in risk in the sense of the formula.

Two asset classes that are regarded as diversifiers hardly fulfil this role. Real estate shares have a correlation of 0.75 with US equities, corporate bonds 0.45. Both carry equity risk. REITs are leveraged, listed companies, and with corporate bonds the credit spread widens precisely when equities fall.

The strongest opposite movement in the matrix is shown by commodities and long-term government bonds, at −0.34. This opposite movement has a common cause to which the two asset classes react with opposite signs. Rising commodity prices mean inflation, inflation leads to rising interest rates, and rising interest rates lower bond prices.

bloecke.unter: The further left an asset class is, the more it contributes to reducing risk; its position says nothing about its return.

bloecke.md:
Putting 50% each into US equities and equities from other developed markets (ρ = 0.87) mathematically gives a volatility of 16.06%, while the weighted average is 16.61%. The saving is 0.55 percentage points.

The same 50/50 mix of US equities and long-term government bonds (ρ = −0.07) gives 10.21% instead of 14.96%. Here the saving is 4.74 percentage points, almost nine times as much.

A portfolio made up of a world, a Europe and a technology ETF is therefore hardly diversified. It contains the same risk three times, with three sets of fees.

## Causes of rising correlations in crises

In 1995, Longin and Solnik showed for international equity markets that correlation rises with volatility and is therefore not a constant. The pattern has recurred in every crisis since. Three causes work together here.

1. In periods of stress, a common factor dominates. In calm periods, different investments react to different news, such as quarterly results or crop reports. Under stress, they all depend on the same variable, the price of risk. If the required risk premium rises, everything that carries such a premium falls.
2. Forced sales transmit the shock. Margin calls, fund redemptions and risk limits force sales wherever liquidity is still available, that is, precisely in the positions that have *not yet* fallen. The contagion runs through the seller's balance sheet and not through the fundamentals.
3. Part of the rise is a measurement artefact. If correlation is calculated only from observations with extreme moves, it comes out systematically higher than over the whole period, even when the underlying relationship is unchanged. This part is a statistical effect rather than contagion, but for planning purposes that makes no difference.

Robust before-and-after figures for individual crises are rare, because the result depends heavily on how the crisis period is defined. The direction of the finding is undisputed; its magnitude is not.

According to the textbook rule, government bonds cushion falling share prices. In 2022, the opposite happened. The yield on ten-year German federal bonds rose by 274 basis points over the year, from −0.21% to +2.53% (Bundesbank). For a ten-year zero-coupon bond bought at the start of the year, this meant a calculated price loss of around 22% by the end of the year. In the same year, the MSCI World in euros lost 12.78%. The part of the portfolio considered safe therefore lost more than the risky part.

The correlation between equities and bonds depends on the market regime. If the shock comes from demand (2008, 2020), interest rates fall and bonds rise. If it comes from inflation (2022), interest rates rise and both asset classes lose. A correlation close to zero, measured from 2008 to 2021, therefore describes only this one regime and not a fixed property of the two asset classes.

Cash in a drawer is uncorrelated with everything and still not an investment. From 2008 to 2026, gold had a correlation of ρ = 0.08 with US equities, and at 17.58% its volatility was higher than that of the equity index itself. Over the long period from 1900 to 2025, gold returned around 1.3% a year in real terms (Dimson/Marsh/Staunton), compared with 6.6% for US equities. Adding gold lowers volatility and at the same time the expected return. Whether this trade-off is worthwhile cannot be read from any correlation figure. It depends on an assumption about expected returns, and this assumption is considerably more uncertain than any correlation estimate.

- For planning, you should work with crisis correlations and not with average correlations. For all investments that carry a risk premium, that is, equities, high-yield bonds, real estate shares, crypto assets and stakes in private businesses, ρ ≈ 1 is the more realistic assumption in a real crisis.
- The most reliable uncorrelated building block in a German portfolio is an instant-access savings account or a short-dated government bond, not an exotic product. The correlation there is zero because these investments barely fluctuate, not because they move in the opposite direction. For deposits, statutory deposit protection also applies up to €100,000 per customer and institution.
- Weights should not be optimised to the second decimal place of an estimated correlation. The estimation error is larger than the difference the fine-tuning makes to the result.
- The figures in this lesson are calculated in US dollars. For a euro portfolio, the exchange rate noticeably changes volatilities and correlations, especially for bonds.

bloecke.titel: Measurement frequency, period and rank correlation
bloecke.md:
Daily returns often give lower correlations than monthly or annual returns, because short-term noise masks the common trend. For investors with a horizon of decades, annual returns would be more meaningful. But there are too few of them, because 30 years give only 30 observations. Monthly data over 15 to 20 years are the usual compromise, which the matrix above also uses.

The commonly used Pearson coefficient measures only linear relationships and is sensitive to outliers. Spearman's rank correlation is more robust. For the question that matters more in practice, whether two investments take extreme values *together*, you need measures of tail dependence or copula models. In everyday use, it is enough to follow the rule of thumb that this dependence is higher than the Pearson value suggests.

mitnehmen: The expected return of a mix is the weighted average, but the risk is not; this is due to the covariance term, the only term in the variance formula that can become negative.

Lowering correlation reduces risk all the more, the lower the correlation already is; in practice, however, it is mainly the positive range that is attainable, because persistently negative correlation combined with a positive expected return hardly ever occurs in reality.
Equity regions correlate with each other at 0.7 to 0.9, which is why regional diversification does avoid cluster risks but lowers volatility only by tenths of a percentage point.
Correlations depend on the market regime; in periods of stress they approach one, and in 2022 the sign between equities and bonds even reversed.
A low correlation says nothing about the expected return, because diversification is a decision about risk and not a means of increasing returns.

begriffe.text: Measure of whether two return series are above or below their respective means at the same time. Its unit is per cent squared, which makes it hard to interpret directly.
Covariance divided by the product of the standard deviations. It is dimensionless, lies between −1 and +1 and measures only linear co-movement.
The third term of the portfolio variance (2·wA·wB·σA·σB·ρ). It is the only part that can become negative and therefore contains the entire mathematical effect of diversification.
The markedly higher correlation between risky assets measured in periods of stress. It arises from common risk factors, from forced sales and partly from measuring on extreme observations.
